blocks.title: The diplomatic landscape was multipolar
paragraphs: Balhae conducted relations with Tang, Silla, Japan and frontier powers including Khitan and other northeastern communities. Diplomatic records survive unevenly, with Japanese and Chinese texts especially important. This imbalance can make named royal embassies appear to be the whole foreign policy, while communications among neighboring communities remain poorly documented.

Each partner offered different possibilities. Tang contact could provide ritual recognition and access to elite goods, learning and markets. Japan was a significant recipient of embassies and could be an additional strategic audience. Relations with Silla involved competition, coexistence and varying kinds of contact rather than permanent hostility. No single diplomatic label explains all the intervals across more than two centuries of statehood.

blocks.title: An embassy as a claim about status
paragraphs: A Balhae mission might deliver a letter, tribute goods, requests or commercial interests while negotiating court ceremony. The wording of diplomatic texts matters because rulers described themselves in ways designed for particular audiences. Some Balhae messages to Japan emphasized connection with Goguryeo and the traditions of Buyeo. This evidence demonstrates a political claim made abroad, not direct proof of the ethnic identity of every subject.

A visiting delegation was also composed of real people facing long journeys. The ability to send specialists capable of producing documents in recognized literary conventions implies institutions of training and material support. But the diary of a court reception does not record every encounter the envoys had during travel, nor the many people who sustained their movement. Diplomacy was an economic and logistical undertaking beyond the exchange of formal titles.

blocks.title: Tang contact despite earlier war
paragraphs: Conflict in the 730s did not prevent later negotiation between Balhae and Tang. Courts used ritual vocabulary that preserved hierarchical distinctions while dealing with rulers who could act independently. The continuing exchange of missions is therefore a warning against defining sovereignty solely by the titles used in imperial documents.

Through diplomacy Balhae could seek information, obtain prestige and open pathways to cultural and commercial resources. Tang also had strategic reasons to manage its relationship with the northeastern kingdom as frontier conditions changed. The political significance of a mission depends on its moment: a formal recognition after a confrontation may accomplish something different from a routine congratulatory embassy in a comparatively peaceful decade.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Japan as partner and observer
paragraphs: Balhae–Japan embassies are particularly valuable for reconstructing the kingdom's external presentation. Japanese court records sometimes preserved the envoys' dates, receptions and exchanges of gifts. They should be read alongside logistical circumstances and changes in Japan's own policies, rather than as a timeless friendship between two modern nations.

Sea travel imposed seasonal limits and risks. A successful mission involved arranging ships, personnel and goods, while failed crossings may be underrepresented in the narrative record. Official contact could also facilitate private acquisition and circulation of objects. The presence of trade within a diplomatic setting does not prove an unrestricted international market, nor does the existence of diplomatic tension show that practical exchange ceased.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: Relations with Silla across the frontier
paragraphs: Balhae's connection to Silla requires attention to geography and to the coexistence of rival claims over the legacy of older kingdoms. The two courts did not occupy the same position relative to Tang, and their strategic priorities were not constant. Claims about a fixed and heavily patrolled border across centuries can exceed the surviving evidence.

The phrase North–South States, often used in Korean historiography, can be a useful reminder that Silla was not the peninsula's only important contemporary state. Yet it should not flatten the distinct structures or populations of the two kingdoms. A history of diplomacy emphasizes actual episodes of contact and conflict, supported by records where available, rather than imagining a permanent early version of a modern divided Korea.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis

blocks.title: What the archives omit
paragraphs: Court historians preserve envoys because missions mattered to legitimacy and interstate protocol. They usually say less about fishermen, traders, captives, religious travellers and families who crossed political boundaries. Archaeological finds of imported or shared material can expand the picture, but cannot by themselves identify the legal status or motivation of a traveller.

It is therefore useful to distinguish confirmed embassies, likely exchange networks and speculative individual journeys. Claims that Balhae was wholly isolated or uniformly cosmopolitan are both oversimplifications. The kingdom occupied a connected northeastern world in which formal ceremonial relations were only one way that people, goods and ideas moved. Its political power rested partly on managing those connections without ever controlling them completely.
